deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is a draft of the material Riemann published as 'Über das Verschwinden der Theta-Functionen' (Crelle 65, 1865/66). Notation: compact Riemann surface of genus p with normalized integrals u_1..u_p. alpha_nu^(mu) = u_nu(eta_mu). The additive constants are fixed so that the Riemann constants k_nu are 0 (assumption from the previous page). Fact from the previous page (Abelian Functions, 1857): if f(z) = theta(u(z) - e) does not vanish identically in z, then it has exactly p zeros eta_1..eta_p and e ≡ sum_{mu=1}^p alpha^(mu) mod periods. Putting z = eta_p gives theta(-sum_1^{p-1} alpha^(mu)) = 0, and by evenness theta(sum_1^{p-1} alpha^(mu)) = 0. Riemann wants this for arbitrary eta_1..eta_{p-1}, but the derivation needs f not identically zero.

(1) Strategy. First prove the identity while eta_1..eta_{p-1} vary independently in open sets. Then extend it everywhere by the identity theorem: an analytic function vanishing on an open set vanishes identically.

(2) Fix a point z. Then e can be chosen with theta(u(z) - e) ≠ 0. Otherwise theta(v) = 0 for all v. In Riemann's normalization theta(v) = sum_m exp(sum a_{mu mu'} m_mu m_mu' + 2 sum m_mu v_mu), which is a Laurent series in e^{2v_1}..e^{2v_p}. All its coefficients exp(a(m,m)) would then vanish, which is false. By continuity, e can then range over an open set U of C^p with theta(u(z) - e) ≠ 0. For such e the function of z is not identically zero, so it has p zeros eta_1..eta_p and e ≡ sum_1^p alpha^(mu).

(3) The map (eta_1..eta_p) -> sum alpha(eta_mu) hits an open set U of values e. Riemann argues this can only happen if the eta's themselves vary independently over open sets. Hence theta(sum_1^{p-1} alpha^(mu)) = 0 holds for eta_1..eta_{p-1} in open sets, and so for all positions by analytic continuation.

(4) Uniqueness of Jacobi inversion. Suppose theta(u(z) - e) is not identically zero in z. Then e ≡ sum_1^p alpha^(mu) can be solved, and only in one way. Suppose another divisor eta' also satisfied the congruence. For each k, theta(u(eta'_k) - e) = theta(-sum_{j≠k} alpha(eta'_j)) = 0 by (3). The function would then vanish at more than p points without being identically zero, which is impossible.

(5) The identically vanishing case. Introduce auxiliary point pairs (eta_mu, epsilon_mu). Consider theta(u + alpha(eta_1) - alpha(epsilon_1) - e), then theta(u + sum_1^2 alpha(eta) - sum_1^2 alpha(epsilon) - e), and so on. Let m be the step where the version with m-1 pairs vanishes identically (for all z and all auxiliary points) but

  f(z) = theta(u(z) + sum_1^m alpha(eta_mu) - sum_1^m alpha(epsilon_mu) - e)

does not vanish identically. Then f(epsilon_k) = 0 for k = 1..m. Indeed, the argument at z = epsilon_k is the (m-1)-pair expression evaluated at z = eta_m-type data, which vanishes identically. So f has p - m further zeros. The page breaks off here. The next page continues: these remaining zeros together with eta_1..eta_m solve e ≡ sum_1^p alpha, with m+1 of the eta freely choosable. This is the theta-function form of the dimension count of special divisors (Riemann–Roch / Riemann singularity theorem).
errors: The claim in (3) is stated rather than proved: an open set of e forces the eta to fill an open set of the symmetric product. This holds because sum alpha(eta) depends holomorphically on p points, so its image cannot cover an open set unless the points vary over p-dimensional families. Riemann leaves it implicit.

In (4), 'immer' (existence) rests entirely on the previously proved fact that a non-identically-vanishing theta(u-e) has exactly p zeros with e ≡ sum alpha. Multiplicities of coincident points are not discussed; this is acceptable but implicit.
Everything holds only under the normalization that the Riemann constants k vanish. Riemann notes that this restriction is removed later by shifting the argument by -k.

results.what: theta(sum_{mu=1}^{p-1} u(eta_mu)) = 0 for arbitrary eta_1..eta_{p-1} (with k=0), proved by first treating open sets and then using the identity theorem.
results.modern_name: Riemann vanishing theorem (theta divisor = W_{p-1} + Riemann constant)

results.what: Uniqueness and existence of the solution of the Jacobi inversion congruence when theta(u-e) is not identically zero.
results.modern_name: Jacobi inversion / Abel–Jacobi map is birational from Sym^p onto the Jacobian; unique inversion off the special locus

results.what: Treatment of the identically vanishing case via theta(u + sum_1^m alpha(eta) - sum_1^m alpha(epsilon) - e). The least such m gives the number of freely choosable points.
results.modern_name: Riemann singularity theorem / Riemann–Roch dimension of special divisors via theta

results.what: theta is not identically zero, since its Fourier (Laurent in e^{2v}) coefficients are nonzero.
results.modern_name: nontriviality of the Riemann theta function

deep.surprise_reason: This page is a working draft of Riemann's own published 1865 paper on the vanishing of theta functions. The content matches the published arguments, so it adds draft details but no new results.

checkable.sympy: import mpmath; tau=mpmath.mpc(0.3,1.1); q=mpmath.exp(mpmath.pi*1j*tau); abs(mpmath.jtheta(3, mpmath.pi/2+mpmath.pi*tau/2, q)) < 1e-12
checkable.asserts: Genus-1 instance of the vanishing theorem: theta vanishes at the Riemann constant (half-period (1+tau)/2). With k=0 normalization, this is theta(sum over p-1 = 0 points) = 0.
The theta function is even, as used to pass from theta(-sum alpha) = 0 to theta(sum alpha) = 0.

checkable.sympy: import mpmath; tau=mpmath.mpc(0.3,1.1); q=mpmath.exp(mpmath.pi*1j*tau); mpmath.quad(lambda x: mpmath.jtheta(3,mpmath.pi*x,q)*mpmath.exp(-2j*mpmath.pi*x),[0,1])
checkable.asserts: A Fourier coefficient of theta is nonzero (here q^1), so theta is not identically zero (step 2).

transcription_corrections: Line 2: 'nach dem Zusatz' is probably 'nach dem Satze'.
'Sie wird also nur für p Lagen von (η, z) Null' should read approximately 'nur für p Lagen von z Null' (as a function of z).
'für jeden Werth von [...] z, η_1, z [?] verschwindet' should be 'für jeden Werth von z, η_1, ε_1 verschwindet'.
'ϑ(u_1+Σ_1^2 α_1^μ − Σ_1^2 α_1^μ − e_1 …)' denotes Σ_1^2 α_1(η_μ) − Σ_1^2 α_1(ε_μ): the two sums are over the η- and ε-points respectively.
'ϑ(u_1 Σ_0^{m-1} α … − Σ_0^{m-1} …)' should have lower index 1 (Σ_1^{m-1}), with η-values minus ε-values; the second function has Σ_1^m.
'für ε_1,…,ε_m, weil ϑ(Σ_1^m …) identisch verschwindet' is correct as read. The final line should continue 'außerdem also noch für p−m [Punkte]' (continued on the next page).
